characteristics.cultivar: Da Bai, Da Hao, and local cultivars

description.short: The most accessible white tea grade made from mature leaves, full-bodied and especially prized with age
description.overview: Harvested from coarser, mature leaves later in the season, making it the most affordable white tea, yet this very maturity grants it tremendous aging potential.
description.leaf: Large, mature leaves with few buds, dark green to brownish in color
description.liquor: Ranges from bright yellow (young tea) to deep amber (aged tea)
description.aroma: Grassy and hay-like when young, evolving into jujube date and honey aromas with years of storage
description.taste: Full-bodied and rustic when young; softens and sweetens with age, developing rich dried-fruit nuances
description.aftertaste: Moderate; warm, sweet, and comforting in aged versions
description.processing: Harvesting mature leaves (sometimes with a sparse proportion of buds) → prolonged withering → slow drying without fixation or rolling

history.origin: Historically viewed as a residual grade of white tea — composed of whatever was plucked after the prized buds and young leaves were selected for Bai Hao Yin Zhen and Bai Mu Dan.
history.development: Long regarded as an everyday, rustic beverage consumed domestically or brewed for folk health remedies.
history.modern: With the surge of interest in aged white tea during the 2010s, Shou Mei underwent a dramatic re-evaluation — today, aged pressed Shou Mei tea cakes (similar to pu-erh) form a prominent collectible category.
interestingFacts: In Fujian folklore, Shou Mei was traditionally drunk to cool internal heat and soothe inflammation, contributing to its name 'Longevity Eyebrow.'
Due to affordable raw material costs and its rich composition suited for aging, Shou Mei is the white tea most commonly pressed into cakes for long-term storage like pu-erh.
